entries.title: Advocates oppose Nicor's $220M proposed rate hike
entries.summary: <p>Consumer advocates want <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2026/01/09/nicor-rate-hike-gas-bill-increase-illinois" >Nicor Gas to cut its proposed $220.8 million rate hike</a> by 80%, saying the company is overzealous in seeking profit.</p><p>Advocates are seeking a $178 million cut to the proposal, according to filings to the Illinois Commerce Commission from the Illinois Attorney General’s office and groups like the Citizens Utility Board and Illinois PIRG. </p><p>They say the utility company's estimates are “overstated” and “inappropriate.”</p><p>But it is ultimately up to the Illinois Commerce Commission, which may rule later this year on the company’s request. Nicor's proposal could bump gas bills by an average of $72 per year for the company’s 2.3 million customers across the northern part of the state.</p><p>“We’re asking the ICC to make this wealthy monopoly live within its means like the rest of us,” said Eric DeBellis, counsel for the Citizens Utility Board, a nonprofit consumer advocate group, at a Monday news conference.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2026/01/09/nicor-rate-hike-gas-bill-increase-illinois" >Nicor seeks another massive rate hike that could add $6 to suburban gas bills</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2025/11/19/nicor-rate-hike-suburban-natural-gas-customers-illinois-commerce-commission-reduction" >ICC slashes Nicor’s proposed $314 million rate hike for suburban gas customers</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Nicor's proposal, filed earlier this year, was submitted less than two months after the Illinois Commerce Commission <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2025/11/19/nicor-rate-hike-suburban-natural-gas-customers-illinois-commerce-commission-reduction" >approved a separate $168 million rate increase</a> for the company. That increase raised average monthly bills by $4.25, though it was still a 47% cut from the company's original 2025 proposal.</p><p>The groups argue that Nicor's increase in capital spending is driving the rising costs. They say that spending could be cut by $97 million.</p><p>Nicor’s capital spending skyrocketed in 2015 after a state law temporarily gave it license to do so while replacing its leak-prone cast iron pipes.</p><p>The consumer groups say Nicor replaced the last cast iron pipe in 2018, but has continued spending three times as much annually prior to the temporary law’s passage. Meanwhile, household gas usage has decreased 26% statewide.</p><p>Illinois PIRG Director Abe Scarr said the company wants to “create a new normal of spending” by keeping up capital costs without the projects to back it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-980000" name="image-980000"></a> entries.title: Brewers bash Shota Imanaga, still look capable of being team in Cubs’ way
entries.summary: <p>Is this week’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>-Brewers clash for control of the National League Central just another series in mid-May?</p><p>“There’s definitely some big series in September,” Cubs outfielder <b>Ian Happ </b>said before the three-game set opened Monday night at Wrigley Field. “You maybe have a group coming in who you’re close to in the divisional race or close in the standings.</p><p>“But early in the season — I know there’s going to be a lot made of this series — it’s another series of baseball.”</p><p>The Cubs might think that way, but don’t tell the Brewers, who brought their big bats south to remind everyone they’re still the three-time reigning division champs. With a 9-3 pummeling of their rivals in the teams’ first meeting of the season, they struck a familiar blow — several, in fact — against Cubs starter <b>Shota Imanaga</b>, bringing to mind the beatdowns they handed out last October when they knocked out the Cubs.</p><p>In Game 2 of the NL Division Series, Imanaga allowed four runs and two homers and was gone after just eight outs. Monday was worse. The Japanese southpaw was tagged for eight runs and nine hits, including a pair of moonshot homers off the right-field video board. He lasted 4 „ innings, a rare 2026 clunker.</p><p>“Shota just didn’t have a good night,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “He just didn’t have real good command — the command that he usually has. . . . It was, frankly, not being able to put the ball where he wanted to put it.”</p><p>Through an interpreter, Imanaga gave this assessment: “Overall, their game plan overcame my skills.”</p><p>Hasn’t that so often been the case for the small-market Brewers in their recent matchups with the Cubs? Even with the Cubs’ offseason spending and World Series goals, it was still Brewers on top.</p><p>“The Brewers are the team that’s won the division for the last three years — that’s what we want to do,” Counsell said. “Last year, they beat us, and they had a fabulous season. We’ve got to improve to get there.”</p><h3>Fixing Phil</h3><p>Reliever <b>Phil Maton </b>was perhaps the biggest addition as <b>Jed Hoyer’s</b> front office remade the Cubs’ bullpen last winter. But so far, he has been a big bugaboo on a pitching staff that already has no shortage of question marks.</p><p>Maton, whose two-year, $14.5 million contract makes him the highest-paid member of the relief corps, coughed up the go-ahead three-run homer Sunday in the eighth inning of the Cubs’ loss to the White Sox, his latest bumpy outing. It was the sixth time in 14 appearances this season he has allowed more than one run.</p><p>The 10-year veteran had figured to be reliable, with a 3.33 ERA across his previous four seasons. Instead, he has a 9.49 ERA midway through his second month as a Cub.</p><p>“I’m incredibly frustrated,” Maton said Monday. “You’re brought over here, and there’s a lot of responsibility to not only pitch well but get the game going in the right direction. And I feel there’s been lots of situations where Craig’s trusted me in tight ballgames and I just haven’t gotten it done. That’s the hardest part.”</p><p>Counsell said it’s a matter of restoring Maton’s confidence so he can deliver in the types of situations the Cubs envisioned when they added him.</p><p>“Phil got burned by some off-speed pitches earlier in the season, and it’s made him a little gun-shy with some of his best pitches,” Counsell said. “We’ve got to get him back to full confidence in his full repertoire.”</p><div class="PageListC" data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-b20000" entries.title: White Sox manager Will Venable ejected after two tough calls by umps in loss at Seattle
entries.summary: <p>A pair of questionable calls by the umpiring crew were enough to get generally unflappable <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> manager Will Venable ejected from Monday’s series-opening 6-1 loss to the Mariners.</p><p>The second-year skipper lost his cool in the third inning after Randy Arozarena swatted a double to left field off Sox starter Noah Schultz with Jhonny Pereda on first.</p><p>Pereda took a wide turn around second, crossing paths and stumbling past second baseman Sam Antonacci baserunner before rounding third. Left fielder Tristan Peters had the baserunner dead to rights at home, but the crew ruled Antonacci had interfered with Pereda and gave Seattle a run for a 2-0 lead.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Will Venable has been tossed after back-to-back questionable calls by the umps in Seattle <a href="https://t.co/1EdOZEA2cj">pic.twitter.com/1EdOZEA2cj</a></p>— Sox On 35th (@SoxOn35th) <a href="https://twitter.com/SoxOn35th/status/2056567522053222837?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The controversial two-out call came a play after umps denied a possible double-play liner that Antonacci seemed to catch and then intentionally drop. Crew chief Tripp Gibson ruled it a lineout, but Pereda didn’t appear to tag up either way.</p><p>It was all enough to get the usually laid-back Venable to toss his hat on the field in frustration, earning his first heave-ho of the season and fourth of his career.</p><p>The calls might’ve loomed larger if M’s third baseman Colt Emerson hadn’t put the game out of reach with a three-run homer in the eighth inning off reliever Trevor Richards. Peters plated the Sox’ only run with a sixth-inning solo blast.</p><p>Bench coach Walker McKinven ran things for the Sox in Venable’s stead.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox players can relate to Pete Crow-Armstrong's frustration with chirping fans, but not his tantrum
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Basking in the glow of their Crosstown Series win, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> players were too busy replaying clips of Edgar Quero walking off the Cubs to spend time on the viral video of Pete Crow-Armstrong’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/18/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-heckler-white-sox-fan-crosstown-rivalry-viral" >offensive response to a heckler</a> Sunday at Rate Field.</p><p>But they’re no strangers to the sort of vitriol that gets peppered from the stands onto any player within earshot.</p><p>“You can’t tune everything out,” said Andrew Benintendi, who has gotten more than his share of earfuls in 11 seasons. “You’ll hear things I’m sure you don’t like, but whatever.</p><p>“It’s just words.”</p><p>That’s where a healthy dose of Zen is vital for any big-leaguer to cope with the torrents of verbal abuse from fans who are more emboldened in the age of social media, according to the veteran.</p><p>“You can crap-talk a player or whatever — that stuff’s going to happen,” Benintendi said. “There’s definitely a line … and, obviously, I think fans now cross that line a lot more than they used to. So I guess every player has their own line, so they have to determine what that is.”</p><p>Miguel Vargas, who roped the two-run double that preceded PCA’s outburst, hadn’t seen the video, but he said he has come close to losing his temper with rowdy fans in the past.</p><p>“I feel a line between respect and disrespect, and I think sometimes people out there don’t know [they] crossed the line,” Vargas said. “And it’s hard to hear that sometimes from fans when you’ve got a family, especially [when your family are] in the stands sometimes too. But we’ve got a great atmosphere with the fans out there.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/17/crosstown-rivalry-gets-spicy-thanks-to-pete-crow-armstrong-and-fan" >Crosstown rivalry gets spicy thanks to Pete Crow-Armstrong and fan</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The comments that got PCA riled up didn’t seem to come anywhere near the personal attack that brought Diamondbacks infielder Ketel Marte to tears at Rate Field last summer when a fan <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/25/diamondbacks-ketel-marte-in-tears-after-fan-at-rate-field-yells-comment-about-late-mother-white-sox" >insulted his late mother</a>.</p><p>The usual fan slander is generally light-hearted and will often get a smile from outfielder Derek Hill, who never ceases to be amazed by fans’ energy.</p><p>“People are very passionate about their teams, and we wouldn’t have it any other way,” Hill said. “It’s pretty crazy how much people love their sports teams. I mean, we all feel it. I love the Chargers and my Chargers are doing good — we all fall into the habits, you know?”</p><p>Hill said his first Cubs-Sox experience was the most ballpark energy he has felt since arriving on the South Side late last season. Wherever he plays, he knows customers will try to get their money’s worth.</p><p>“People come out to the games for a lot of different reasons,” Hill said. “You’ve got some people who come out just because they love the games. People come out because they had a bad day and they want to blow off some steam. Hey, you pay the money to come see us play — cool, do whatever you want to.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago's parking meters could be sold again under deal requiring City Council approval
entries.summary: <p>The owner of Chicago's parking meters is seeking to sell the asset to a New York investment firm — but the deal requires approval from City Council.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's office on Monday confirmed the tentative agreement between Chicago Parking Meters LLC and New York-based Stonepeak Partners. </p><p>The deal, which would change ownership of the meters and who collects their profits, now sits before City Council, which could seek concessions in favor of the city before approving it.</p><p>The tentative sale is the most recent development in the fight for parking assets. </p><p>In January, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/19/chicago-parking-meters-up-for-sale-but-johnson-urged-to-proceed-carefully-on-potential-buy-back" target="_blank" >Johnson considered purchasing</a> the 57 years that remain on the infamous 75-year parking meter deal, made in 2008 under former Mayor Richard M. Daley.</p><p>Doing so would have required the city to borrow billions of dollars. But Johnson later <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/20/mayor-brandon-johnson-parking-meter-deal-dropping-buyback-bid" target="_blank" >dropped the city’s bid</a> after determining the $3 billion asking price, he said then, "would have made a bad deal even worse."</p>

entries.title: White Sox must strike fast to keep Munetaka Murakami before he races off elsewhere — worst of all to Cubs
entries.summary: <p>If the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> haven’t begun negotiating a contract extension for Munetaka Murakami, they should have — yesterday.</p><p>As last weekend’s hugely satisfying spectacle against the Cubs showed, the Japanese slugger is the Sox’ most charismatic star since Tim Anderson, or at least until the Guardians’ Jose Ramirez knocked him into Cuckooland with a single punch in 2023.</p><p>With 17 home runs in just 47 games and 203 plate appearances, Murakami is the unquestionable transformative piece that has made the Sox relevant again. And if they don’t launch a preemptive strike and sign him to an extension sooner rather than later, they’re looking at the next big bidding war for a player the rest of the baseball industry whiffed on last winter, allowing the Sox to sign him for the bargain price of two years, $35 million.</p><p>Sox chairman Jerry Reinsdorf, who made it to his 90th birthday without giving any Sox player a $100 million contract, will need to go well north of that number to keep Murakami, a 26-year-old star entering his prime.</p><p>If not, Reinsdorf could be risking the one doomsday scenario that might cause even the most diehard loyalists to curse the day they ever became Sox fans: Tom Ricketts and the Cubs poaching Murakami away like the Dodgers did with Shohei Ohtani, who forsook the Angels to sign with a winner two years ago.</p><p>“I do think they’re on the clock with him,” said a highly placed industry source with firsthand knowledge of the negotiations with Murakami last winter.</p><p>Murakami’s agent, Casey Close, made it clear to teams early on that he was seeking a deal in the $100 million-plus range when Murakami first became available. But no one was willing to pay that because the industry was convinced his strikeout rate would be unplayably high.</p><p>It reached the point where his agents contacted teams and essentially said, “Make us your best offer. We’ll listen.” The Sox may have been the only team willing to go even that far, which is how Chris Getz, the team’s executive vice president and general manager, was able to land him at a discount rate.</p><p>There is still some risk in giving Murakami an extension now. He’s striking out at a 33% rate (league average is 22%), and if that number closes in on 40% and balls stop leaving the park, teams will be congratulating themselves on taking a pass on him. The prudent course may be for the Sox to wait for the season to play out.</p><p>But if Murakami hits 40 homers or more and his agents are looking for the type of payday — or bigger — that they sought last winter, some in the industry believe the Sox will be priced out.</p><p>Thus the urgency to get Murakami extended now before his cost spirals beyond what the Sox are willing to pay. Yes, he seems very happy on the South Side. He likes his teammates, and they like him. But it would be foolish to count on the Sox receiving a hometown discount. The Angels did everything in their power to make Ohtani feel at home, and still he left for the Dodgers.</p><p>“Tom Ricketts, you have a call on Line 1.”</p><p>The Sun-Times reached out to Getz, who didn’t respond by the time of publication. Close politely declined to comment about possible negotiations involving his client, saying only, “I’m very happy for Mune, and [it’s] fun to watch the Sox compete.”</p><p>Cubs pitcher Jameson Taillon, who raved about Murakami after he took him deep Saturday, was still singing his praises the next day.</p><p>“It’s just a weird thing that 29 of 30 teams all decided together [not to pursue him],” Taillon said. “I’m sure they had their metrics and numbers that they believed in. But that’s where you’ve also got to believe in humans and track record. If the fear is he swings and misses too much, supposedly, if you believe in the human — and everything I’ve heard about him is he’s a good dude and works hard, wants to be really good and is curious — why don’t you believe in the human figuring it out and working with him?</p><p>“When you have, like, 80-grade power, you would just think more teams would bet on the guy to figure out the swing and miss. He’s only 26. It’s not like he’s a finished product, you know?”</p><p>Murakami was the MVP of Nippon Professional Baseball’s Central League in 2021 and ’22. At age 22 in ’22, he also hit 56 home runs and won the Triple Crown.</p><p>He’s the player, someone told Taillon, who’s going to force Reinsdorf to tap his bank account harder than he ever has before — or perhaps lean on his partner and eventual successor, Justin Ishbia.</p><p>“I don’t know what they do on the South Side,” Taillon said. “I mean, you’ve got to think he’s marketable. He puts balls in the seats. That’s a pretty cool thing that can draw attendance and jersey sales and all that. So, yeah, he’d be a good one to invest in. I’m sure there’s gonna be a lot of teams that are interested, too.”</p><p>And if the Cubs were to poach him from the Sox?</p><p>“That’d be nice,” Taillon said. “He’s gonna hit 40 home runs. I mean, who knows? I’m sure his agents probably signed this short-term deal with this scenario playing out perfectly, where they want him to hit free agency again. entries.title: Knee injury knocks White Sox catcher Kyle Teel out of action at least another three weeks
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> won’t get Kyle Teel back for at least another three weeks after their prized catcher sprained a knee ligament during a rehabilitation assignment on his way back from a pulled hamstring.</p><p>The second-year backstop could be out up to six weeks, the Sox announced Monday before their series opener against the Mariners, although it took Teel longer than that to recover from the hammy he pulled while playing for Team Italy during the World Baseball Classic.</p><p>“Happy that it wasn’t a tear or anything,” manager Will Venable said. “With the sprain, hopefully it’s just a matter of weeks and not months that he’s back healthy and running around and playing.”</p><p>It’s a frustrating setback for Teel, 24, who hit .273/.375/.411 with eight homers in 78 games during his rookie campaign last year.</p><p>He had appeared poised for his 2026 debut during this West Coast road trip until <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/17/new-knee-issue-adds-to-intrigue-surrounding-white-sox-catcher-kyle-teel" target="_blank" ><u>tweaking his right knee on Saturday at Triple-A Charlotte</u></a>, during an at-bat in “a softer box” that caught his cleat mid-swing, Venable said.</p><p>That means more time behind the plate for Edgar Quero, who had struggled mightily at the plate until his heroics in Sunday’s Crosstown Classic finale, when he went 3-for-5 with a walkoff home run.</p><p>Drew Romo has also shown surprising pop with four homers in 13 games, but the Sox miss Teel’s glove as much as his bat.</p><p>“Just objectively, not where we want to be defensively, blocking and framing,” Venable said. “There’s things these guys continue to work on very hard.”</p><p></p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: Chicago Reader names new publisher
entries.summary: <p>A third-generation Chicagoan from South Shore will be the Chicago Reader's next publisher.</p><p>Malik Johnson, who was previously the executive director and publisher of South Side Media Works, which oversees South Side Weekly and Hyde Park Herald, will join the newsroom June 1, the publication announced Monday.</p><p>"The Reader has a rich and storied history that stands on its own, and I'm thrilled to help usher in a new beginning for the publication," Jackson said in a news release. </p><p>The Reader was founded in 1971 in the Kenwood neighborhood. In 2018, the Chicago Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/6/15/18327975/chicago-reader-sold-to-group-led-by-chicago-crusader-publisher" target="_blank" >sold the Reader</a> to a group led by Dorothy Leavell, the publisher of the Chicago Crusader and Gary Crusader newspapers.</p><p>In recent years, the paper has struggled to stay afloat. </p><p>In 2022, the Reader nearly shuttered during a dispute among board members over the paper's leadership. The dispute, which prevented the paper's transition to nonprofit ownership, centered around <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/2/14/22927012/chicago-reader-future-tracy-baim-board-infighting-nonprofit-leadership" >concerns about then co-publisher and president, Tracy Baim</a>. By the end of 2022, Baim stepped down from her position. </p><p>In January 2025, the publication laid off six employees to reduce costs and prevent closure. Later that year, the Reader was acquired by Noisy Creek, a media company dedicated to alternative weekly publications such as The Stranger in Seattle and the Portland Mercury<i>.</i></p><p>The paper returned to print in February as monthly magazine instead of a weekly newspaper. </p><p>In an editors note announcing the paper's return in February, editor-in-chief Sarah Conway said the Reader was entering a "new era of Chicago journalism."</p><p>Johnson will replace Amber Nettles as publisher. She previously came into the role in 2024, when the publication divided the roles of Solomon Lieberman, who had previously served as both CEO and publisher. In November 2025, she left to join EmpowerLocal as the chief partnerships officer.</p>
